papers.title: Nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic model for the stress-strain and stress-relaxation in metallic glass
papers.abstract: We develop a nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic (VEP) model for the stress-strain response of metallic glasses by connecting the deformation dynamics with the material relaxation time obtained from independent stress-relaxation measurements. The material is modeled as a Maxwell-type element, with a nonlinear elastic spring and a stretched-exponential dashpot whose behavior is determined from the separate stress-relaxation data. The model captures the effects of temperature and strain rate on the initial elastic response, stress overshoot, post-yield softening, and steady flow. We independently determine the reference material-time function $X_0(\varepsilon)$ from the stress-relaxation response and the nonlinear material-time variable $X(\varepsilon)$ from the elastic-viscoplastic strain decomposition based on the stress-strain response. We introduce an Eyring-type function or material-time ratio $\phi(\varepsilon)=X(\varepsilon)/X_0(\varepsilon)$ which quantifies the change of relaxation dynamics during nonlinear deformation. Our model provides a simple connection between structural relaxation and yielding in metallic glasses.

papers.title: A variational phase-field theory of cohesive fracture at finite deformation
papers.abstract: This paper formulates a kinematically and variationally consistent phase-field theory for cohesive fracture at finite deformation. The theory introduces an independent compliance-damage field, which accommodates both diffuse distributions and singular concentrations. The phase-field is thereby freed from the dual burden of describing crack geometry and material degradation. A rank-one additive split of the deformation gradient makes separation explicit through independent crack-strain and reference-normal fields. All fields are governed by a single principle of minimum potential energy, which consistently couples nonlinear bulk deformation, crack separation, and crack-plane rotation. One-dimensional energy comparisons show that minimization favors Dirac-type concentration of compliance damage and crack strain. Strong displacement discontinuities thus emerge naturally at a finite phase-field length without being prescribed a priori, while the phase-field remains continuous. The concentrated energy recovers the exact bulk--interface structure of a sharp-crack cohesive zone model. General objective hyperelastic bulk potentials and admissible mixed-mode cohesive laws can therefore be prescribed independently, with the nominal traction--separation law unaffected by the bulk law or phase-field length. Diffuse damage can coexist with concentrated cracks, retaining deformation modes for bulk-energy relaxation during nucleation. Two- and three-dimensional examples validate the theory across large stretches, finite rotations, and complex crack paths. Notably, the computed near-tip Cauchy stress closely matches the analytical 1/r crack-tip asymptotic solution of Long et al. (2011) outside the cohesive zone.

papers.title: Chirality inversion and odd transport in a suspension of living rotors
papers.abstract: Chiral symmetry breaking is a defining feature of life, visible at all scales from molecules to organisms. Yet how microscopic chirality propagates to shape the macroscopic properties of living matter remains poorly understood. Here, using a new experimental system of spinning microalgae, we show that a living chiral fluid behaves fundamentally differently from an externally driven one. As their density increases, cells self-assemble hydrodynamically into small rotating clusters which merge into a percolating chiral fluid. Strikingly, microscopic and macroscopic vorticity have opposite signs: individual cells all spin clockwise, yet clusters orbit counterclockwise. Combining experiments, theory and simulations, we show that both chirality inversion and percolation are direct consequences of the cells' internally driven nature. We then show how percolation reshapes transport, with even and odd diffusivities responding differently to the emerging network topology.

papers.title: Integer defects in active nematics of ellipsoidal Quincke rollers
papers.abstract: Transverse propulsion changes topological ordering in dense ellipsoidal Quincke rollers. Under an alternating-current electric field, a polar velocity field coexists with perpendicular nematic particle alignment. The system supports integer +1 velocity vortices with radial particle axes and -1 saddle defects. Oppositely charged defects migrate along domain walls and annihilate as polar domains merge. These results identify propulsion direction relative to particle shape as a control parameter for defect textures and collective ordering.

papers.title: Static and dynamic density correlations of interacting active Brownian particles
papers.abstract: We develop a stochastic Dean--Kawasaki field theory to predict the static structure factor and collective intermediate scattering function of interacting active Brownian particles. Starting from the microscopic overdamped dynamics, we derive coupled stochastic equations for the density and polarization fields using an angular-moment closure. Gaussian linearization then yields closed analytical expressions for static and dynamic density correlations in terms of propulsion speed, mean number density, interaction potential, translational and rotational diffusivities. The coupling between density and polarization predicts a crossover from exponential relaxation to damped oscillations despite the absence of inertia. For Gaussian-core potential, the predictions contain no fitting parameters. Brownian dynamics simulations show quantitative agreement at low activity and long wavelengths, and reproduce the crossover behaviour. For Weeks--Chandler--Andersen potential, the nonintegrable core makes both the Fourier transform of the potential and the self-interaction correction term in the Dean--Kawasaki field theory ill-defined. We therefore introduce an approximation that replaces the interaction potential with a passive direct-correlation function fitted separately at each density and temperature. This approximation requires no additional activity-dependent fitting parameters.

papers.title: Microswimmers lose by swimming selfishly
papers.abstract: At low Reynolds number, microswimmers are coupled by the flows they create, even when they are apart. The best way for each swimmer to push itself forward then depends on its neighbors, turning swimming together into a game. To study this, we optimize the shape changes of soft swimmers, alone and in pairs, with a differentiable Stokes solver. From random initial membrane motions, a lone swimmer converges to a traveling membrane wave. In a pair, the stroke of a swimmer affects its neighbor far more than the neighbor affects its own best stroke. For swimmers in line, this influence decays as $1/\ell$ with their separation $\ell$, whereas the incentive to respond decays as $1/\ell^2$. Selfish swimmers, which maximize their own payoff, respond only to the weak incentive. The cooperative gain they miss decays only as $1/\ell^2$, and their selfish adaptations leave the pair worse off than if both had kept their solitary strokes. Related swimmers, which also value the payoff of their neighbor, recover this gain, whereas competitors pay to hinder each other, both following a law that we derive analytically. Hydrodynamics alone thus makes swimming in company a social dilemma, whose outcome depends on how much the swimmers value each other.

papers.title: Drying kinematics selects open honeycomb fold networks on solvent-extracted viscoelastic thin films and gels
papers.abstract: Solvent extraction and drying of substrate-supported viscoelastic films and gels produce quasiperiodic networks of three-armed surface folds. In this Letter, we examine the physical mechanisms governing their formation, length scales, and geometric organization. We observed that swelling-induced compression in the pinned film drives localized folding of a stiffening, diffusively thickening surface skin over a drained underlayer. Combining experiments and theory, we reveal that both the pattern wavelength and fold-arm length scale with the dried-film thickness following a power-law with an exponent 5/8, with remarkably weak dependence on elastic modulus. The folds form 120-degree junctions on a triangular lattice, defining an open honeycomb network whose pitch satisfies p = sqrt(3)(aL + g), where g is the junction gap. Notably, the folds accommodate less than 0.1% of the stored compressive strain, implicating elastocapillary arrest, rather than strain relaxation, in limiting their amplitude. These findings establish distinct geometric, kinetic, and interfacial constraints governing pattern selection in drying soft solids.

papers.title: Flow-polarity decoupling and universal mobility enhancement in dense bacterial active fluids
papers.abstract: Active fluids consisting of living cells or synthetic microswimmers display rich emergent behavior and nonequilibrium mechanical properties, which not only shed light on various biological processes but also inform the engineering of autonomous fluidics and self-driven materials. The individual behavior of microswimmers and their interaction with self-generated mesoscale solvent flows underlie the emergent properties of active fluids. Here we studied the microscopic dynamics in dense 3D bacterial active fluids by simultaneous imaging of cell body, flagella, and flow field. A surprising finding is that the polarity of cells was randomly distributed in mesoscale flow regimes, and yet the system displays mesoscale order in the self-generated solvent flows. Despite the apparent flow-polarity decoupling, the motion of cells relative to local solvent flows predominantly navigated upstream, with the self-advection speed overall enhanced by a flow-controlled constant. Numerical modeling with full hydrodynamic interactions reveals that the observed flow-polarity decoupling arises from the breakdown of the commonly held force-dipole assumption for anisotropic microswimmers: in the presence of flow gradient and near-field hydrodynamic interactions, the direction of total active forcing exerted by a swimming bacterium to the surrounding fluid no longer aligns with its polarity. The simulations suggest that near-field interactions serve as a new type of emergent, configuration-dependent active forcing, which profoundly impact self-organization and transport in dense bacterial suspensions. Taken together, our work establishes fundamental knowledge for faithfully understanding the collective behavior of dense polar active fluids.

papers.title: Optimal chemotactic navigation in disordered landscapes
papers.abstract: Active navigation in disordered landscape with random traps arises from the interplay between directed motion and environmental constraints. Using E. coli chemotactic navigation in agar gels as a model system, we reveal a fundamental trade-off between diffusive exploration and chemotactic directional bias that dictates the optimal strategy for population range expansion. Counter-intuitively, evolution selects for shorter mean run times ({\tau}_f) to achieve faster chemotactic migration in denser environments. Controlled experiments reveal a non-monotonic relationship between chemotactic navigation speed and {\tau}_f, with the optimum shifting according to the density of physical traps in the gel. Single-cell analysis indicates that cells primarily escape a trap without an intervening tumble and without a large reorientation. Based on these observations, we develop a minimal theoretical model showing that the optimal {\tau}_f emerges from an antagonistic scaling: while the diffusion coefficient increases with {\tau}_f, the chemotactic bias coefficient decreases with it. This work establishes an optimal condition for biased run-tumble motion in disordered landscapes with random traps.

papers.title: Exact Generalized Langevin Dynamics of Pair Coordinates in Elastic Networks
papers.abstract: Generalized Langevin equations (GLEs) provide a powerful framework for describing slow dynamics in soft-matter systems, but deriving an exact GLE for a reaction coordinate from an underlying many-body system remains generally difficult. Here, we analytically derive an exact coupled GLE for the overdamped dynamics of two tagged beads in arbitrary harmonic elastic networks. We further derive an exact GLE for their relative coordinate. The memory kernel and effective restoring force are expressed explicitly in terms of the network matrices, thereby providing a systematic reduction of the high-dimensional network dynamics to a pair coordinate. Within the small-displacement approximation, we further derive a GLE for the inter-bead distance, a central observable in distance-sensitive single-molecule experiments. These results therefore have broad potential applications in modeling proteins and other soft-matter systems.

papers.title: Ordering and Defect Dynamics in Passive and Active Nematopolars
papers.abstract: The coexistence of polar and nematic interactions, observed in a broad range of biological and synthetic active systems, gives rise to a rich phenomenology that continues to challenge our theoretical understanding of non-equilibrium collective behaviour. In this paper, we numerically investigate phase ordering and defect dynamics in a newly introduced minimal single-field model for dry nematopolar systems, where competing polar and nematic contributions enter the free energy, and activity is implemented through self-advection. At optimal balance, the system develops depolarization strings connecting half-integer defects and separating domains with opposite polarization, together with closed depolarization loops. We first characterize the elementary relaxation mechanisms of defect pairs and loops, showing that the interplay between polar and nematic alignment gives rise to non-monotonic string-mediated interactions, finite equilibrium separations and distinct loop-collapse pathways. Large-scale simulations from disordered states instead show dynamic scaling with a characteristic length growing as $\sim(t/\ln t)^{1/2}$, consistent with coarsening in systems with non-conserved order parameters and point-like defects. Upon introducing self-advection, sufficiently strong activity leads to the coexistence of positive integer and negative half-integer defects, which we term motility-induced charge symmetry breaking, and to saturation of the characteristic length scales, ultimately resulting in arrested coarsening. Overall, our results provide a simple unified framework for understanding the ordering and defect dynamics in biological and synthetic nematopolar systems.
